newsitem.title: USA: Southwest Air worries about '97 fuel costs.
newsitem.headline: Southwest Air worries about '97 fuel costs.

text.p: Southwest Airlines Chief Financial Officer Gary Kelly said he was concerned high jet fuel prices would put a dent in first quarter earnings but said cost reduction programs could bring substantial savings.
Kelly said jet fuel costs are currently at $0.78 a gallon, up from an average of $0.73 in the last three months of 1996 and from around $0.60 in the first quarter last year.
"That's a very significant increase. There's just no way around that being a painful impact if it stays at that level," he told reporters on a conference call.
"Our hope is that by the time the cold weather season gets behind us and there is less pressure to produce heating oil, that those (jet fuel) prices will come down," Kelly said.
But he said the carrier's outlook for 1997 remains "good," especially if fuel prices stabilized at lower levels.
Southwest Air earlier reported fourth quarter earnings of $28.2 million, or $0.19 per share, compared with $43.4 million, or $0.29 per share, in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Profits for the full year rose to a record $207.3 million, or $1.37 per share, from $182.6 million, or $1.23 per share.
Kelly said the higher fuel costs and a 4.3 cents per gallon fuel tax accounted for the decline in fourth quarter profits, and the carrier has begun a series of cost-cutting programs.

Purchasing initiatives should bring annual savings of $15-20 million starting in 1997 and changes to Southwest Air's reservations sytems should save anywhere between $5 million and $15 million per year from 1998, Kelly said.
Other inititatives would target savings in the operations and maintenance divisions, he said.
Kelly said Southwest's capacity would rise about nine percent in 1997 as it takes delivery of 19 new Boeing Co 737 jets and retires four of its oldest jets.
He said the low-fare carrier would consider raising prices if fuel costs remain very high but that it preferred not to.
"We try to resist those kinds of temptations. We think in the long run that keeping fares low is the best way to maximize revenues," Kelly said.
But he added: "Certainly, over time, if we find that our costs settle in around these kinds of fuel price levels, then we would need to make some adjustments."
